title: Clean-data sleeves and the PEAD beta test
hypothesis: At least one S&P single-name sleeve has standalone alpha after costs.
question: On clean, single-vintage data, did momentum, PEAD or reversion clear its pre-set gate, and was PEAD's return alpha or market beta?
prior: Same priors as v27; the test was whether they survive measurement on clean data.
citations: Bernard, V. & Thomas, J. (1989). Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift. JAR 27.
McLean, R. D. & Pontiff, J. (2016). Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability? JF 71(1).
method: 2013 → 2026-06, cache-consistent, sanitised prices; MOO T+1, 7 bps.
PEAD regressed on SPY daily returns; block-bootstrap of its Sharpe.
verdict_reason: No sleeve cleared its gate and none beat buy-and-hold SPY. Momentum earned Sharpe 0.17, reversion was negative, and PEAD's 0.24 was market beta: alpha −3.25% a year (t = −1.21), beta 0.36.
lessons: The S&P 500 is the lowest-dispersion, most-arbitraged universe; daily single-name edges are smaller than costs.
Always regress a long-biased sleeve on the market before calling it alpha.
This result ended the single-stock program and led to the cross-asset pivot.
footer: Research code is private; methods summarised below.
